title: The technological frontier in fall management for older adults with dementia: A scoping review of prediction, detection, and prevention systems

sections.title: Falls as a geriatric syndrome representing a public health imperative

paragraphs.en: Falls among older adults are increasingly recognized as a multifactorial geriatric syndrome with profound clinical, societal, and economic consequences [1]. Approximately one-third of community-dwelling adults aged ≥65 years experience at least one fall annually, with 20%–30% sustaining moderate-to-severe injuries such as lacerations, fractures, and traumatic brain injuries [2]. Beyond acute injury, falls often initiate a cascade of functional decline characterized by fear of falling, reduced mobility, deconditioning, loss of independence, diminished quality of life, and premature institutionalization in long-term care facilities [3]. Prolonged periods spent on the floor following a fall, known as the ‘long lie’ phenomenon, further increase the risk of serious complications, hypothermia, dehydration, pressure injuries, pneumonia, hospitalization, and mortality [4].

The societal burden of falls extends beyond their clinical consequences. In the United States alone, annual direct medical expenditures attributable to falls exceed US$80 billion, with costs projected to surpass $101 billion by 2030 [1]. Similar economic pressures have been reported internationally, including an estimated annual cost of £4.4 billion to the United Kingdom’s National Health Service for fall-related fractures [5]. Together, these findings underscore the need for effective strategies to prevent falls and facilitate timely intervention when falls occur.

sections.title: Falls in people living with dementia

paragraphs.en: Although falls are common among older adults, people living with dementia experience a disproportionately greater burden. Compared with cognitively intact older adults, people living with dementia are two-to-three times more likely to fall and nearly four times more likely to experience recurrent falls [6]. Recent meta-analyses estimate an annual fall prevalence of 44.3% among individuals with Alzheimer's disease, with some studies reporting fall rates approaching 80% [6].

This heightened vulnerability reflects the multifactorial pathophysiology of dementia. Progressive neurodegeneration disrupts motor control and gait, resulting in impaired balance, increased postural sway, reduced gait velocity, and mediolateral instability [7]. Concurrent impairments in function, attention, visuospatial processing, and judgment further compromise the ability to recognize hazards and safely navigate complex environments [8]. behavioral and psychological symptoms, including wandering, agitation, and restlessness, increase exposure to hazardous situations [9], while polypharmacy, particularly the use of psychotropic medications and antihypertensive agents, further elevates fall risk through sedation, dizziness, and orthostatic hypotension [10,11].

sections.title: Digital technologies for fall management: Rationale for the review

paragraphs.en: In response to this growing clinical challenge, gerontechnology has produced an expanding range of digital solutions designed to support fall prediction, detection, and prevention [12]. These technologies aim to promote safe and independent aging, improve quality of life, reduce caregiver burden, and alleviate pressure on healthcare systems. However, the populations most likely to benefit from these innovations often face the greatest barriers to their successful implementation. Cognitive impairment, behavioral symptoms, resistance to routine changes, and sensory sensitivities may limit sustained engagement with digital technologies, particularly wearable devices [13,14]. Consequently, technological performance demonstrated under controlled laboratory conditions may not translate into meaningful clinical benefit. Successful implementation therefore depends not only on algorithmic performance, but also on usability, acceptability, ethical deployment, and seamless integration into routine dementia care.

Despite rapid technological advances, the evidence specific to people living with dementia remains fragmented. Previous reviews have examined fall management technologies in older adults more broadly [15] or summarized digital technologies across dementia and mild cognitive impairment populations [16]. However, to our knowledge, no review has comprehensively mapped and synthesized the primary literature specifically evaluating digital technologies for fall prediction, detection, and prevention, tailored for people living with dementia.

Accordingly, this scoping review aims to map and synthesize the current evidence on digital fall management technologies for people living with dementia. Specifically, we sought to (1) characterize the existing evidence across fall prediction, detection, and prevention technologies; (2) identify methodological, technological, and implementation challenges affecting their translation into clinical practice; and (3) highlight emerging opportunities, including artificial intelligence, multimodal sensing, and user-centered design, to inform future research and technology development.

This scoping review was conducted in accordance with the methodological framework originally proposed by Arksey and O'Malley (2005) and the updated guidance from the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) for scoping reviews [17,18]. This review is reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR), and the completed checklist is provided in Table A in S1 Appendix. Given the iterative nature of scoping reviews and the absence of a standard requirement for prospective registration, this review was not preregistered.

Consistent with JBI recommendations, formal methodological quality appraisal or risk-of-bias assessment was not undertaken because the objective was to comprehensively map the breadth, characteristics, and knowledge gaps within the available literature rather than evaluate intervention effectiveness.

A systematic literature search was conducted across five electronic databases: Scopus, MEDLINE (Ovid), Embase (Ovid), APA PsycINFO (Ovid), and CINAHL (EBSCO). Searches were limited to peer-reviewed studies published between January 2015 and July 2025 to capture contemporary developments in digital fall management technologies.

The search strategy combined controlled vocabulary (e.g., Medical Subject Headings) and free-text keywords using Boolean operators across three conceptual domains: (1) falls and fall risk (e.g., “falls,” “accidental falls,” “fall risk,”); (2) dementia (e.g., “dementia,” “Alzheimer disease,” “cognitive impairment”); and (3) technology-based Interventions (e.g., “technology,” “wearable electronic devices,” “sensors,” “machine learning,” “virtual reality”). A complete search string for MEDLINE via OVID is provided in the Table B in S1 Appendix.
To maximize retrieval, reference lists of all included studies and relevant review articles were manually screened for additional eligible publications.

Inclusion criteria were: (1) studies published in English involving technologies that are specifically designed for older adults, typically defined as individuals aged 65 or older, with a formal diagnosis of dementia; (2) mixed-population studies if data for people living with dementia outcomes were approximated by simulations performed by healthy individuals; (3) studies that evaluated, described, or implemented a specific technology designed for fall prediction, detection, or prevention; (4) at least one fall-related outcome measured, such as a validated fall risk factor (e.g., gait speed, balance), a fall event itself, or an outcome related to a fall prevention intervention (e.g., reduced fall rate, improved balance post-intervention); (5) original research articles, including cohort studies, case-control studies, feasibility or pilot studies, and diagnostic accuracy studies.

Exclusion criteria were: (1) studies designed exclusively for mild cognitively impaired or healthy older adults; (2) interventions limited to non-technological approaches, such as pharmaceutical or behavioral strategies without a technological component; (3) studies classified as gray literature (e.g., conference abstracts, editorials, dissertations).

Search results were imported into Covidence for screening and study management. Title and abstract screening was independently performed by AK and MB, followed by an independent full-text review by the same reviewers. Disagreements were resolved through discussion, with SN acting as a third reviewer when consensus could not be reached.

sections.title: Data extraction, charting, and synthesis framework

paragraphs.en: A standardized data extraction form was developed to extract study characteristics, including publication details, study design, country, participant characteristics (sample size, dementia subtype, and disease severity), technology characteristics (device type, sensor modality, form factor, and intended purpose), algorithmic approach, performance outcomes, and caregiver involvement.

Given the anticipated heterogeneity in study designs, technologies, populations, and outcome measures, quantitative meta-analysis was neither appropriate nor intended. Instead, a narrative thematic synthesis was undertaken to map the existing evidence and identify recurring patterns, methodological limitations, and knowledge gaps.

Studies were organized according to the primary function of the technology within the fall management continuum: (1) fall prediction and risk stratification, referring to technologies designed to identify individuals at increased risk of future falls; (2) fall detection and emergency response, encompassing technologies that identify fall events in real time and initiate an alert or response; and (3) fall prevention and proactive intervention, including technologies intended to reduce fall risk or improve mobility and safety.

Within each category, technologies were further classified according to their sensing modality (e.g., wearable or ambient systems) to facilitate comparison across technological approaches. This framework enabled a structured synthesis of the current evidence while identifying methodological limitations, research gaps, and future opportunities in digital fall management for people living with dementia.

The databases search identified 207 articles. Following automatic duplicate removal in Covidence, 150 unique records underwent title and abstract screening. After excluding 98 records, 52 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility, of which thirteen studies met the inclusion criteria and were included in the final synthesis. The study selection process is summarized in Fig 1.

The characteristics of the included studies are summarized in Table 1. Thirteen studies published between 2015 and 2025 were included, encompassing a wide range of study designs, clinical settings, and participant populations. Sample size varied considerably, from small feasibility studies involving three healthy volunteers simulating dementia-related movement patterns [19] to larger diagnostic accuracy studies involving more than 30 residents with Alzheimer’s disease [20].

Study populations were heterogenous. Six studies evaluated technologies exclusively using healthy adults or student volunteers performing simulated falls or dementia-related movements [19,21–25], whereas the remaining studies recruited people living with dementia from inpatient, long-term care, assisted living, or community settings [20,26–31].

Dementia subtype and severity were inconsistently reported. Alzheimer’s disease was the most frequently specified diagnosis, whereas several studies included participants with unspecified dementia or younger-onset dementia [30]. Where reported, disease severity ranged from early-stage dementia to moderate and severe dementia in specialized care units [26]. Most clinical studies enrolled fewer than 100 participants.

Sex distribution was also variably reported. Some studies included predominantly female cohorts, for example, Can and colleagues [31] reported over 90% female participants in the intervention group, while others indicated more balanced distributions [26,27]. In contrast, several simulation-based studies did not provide sex data for participants [19,24].

Caregiver involvement was reported primarily in studies involving clinical dementia populations, including nursing staff, formal caregivers, and, less frequently, family caregivers [20,26,27]. In contrast, simulation studies with healthy volunteers did not incorporate caregiver perspectives, with one exception where system design considered caregiver alerts despite their absence from validation procedures [24].

The technological characteristics of the included studies are summarized in Table 2. The identified technologies addressed three principal functions within the fall management continuum: fall prediction and risk stratification, real-time fall detection and alerting, and fall prevention.

Most wearable systems incorporated inertial sensors, including accelerometers, gyroscopes, and inertial measurement units (IMUs) [21,23,24,28]. Ambient monitoring technologies employed radar, depth cameras, red, green, blue (RGB) wavelength cameras, and depth cameras [20,25,26,29–31], while several studies combined multimodal inputs, including radar with real-time pattern recognition [31], and depth cameras integrated with radio-frequency identification (RFID) sensors [26].

Reporting mechanisms involved caregiver notifications, clinician dashboards, or automated alarms; in clinical and assisted living settings, systems were directly integrated with staff workflows to ensure timely emergency response [27,29,31]. In contrast, simulation-based prototypes often restricted outputs to real-time laboratory alerts or offline model validation [19,21,22].

Algorithmic complexity varied substantially. Some studies relied on threshold- or rule-based models [22,25], whereas others implemented machine learning classifiers, including decision trees, random forests, support vector machines (SVMs), AdaBoost, multilayer perceptron, and other ensemble learning methods [21,24,26].

Technology maturity also differed considerably. Several studies evaluated commercially deployed systems within long-term care or assisted-living settings [20,27–31], whereas others focused on laboratory prototypes undergoing preliminary technical validation [19,21–25].

Performance outcomes varied substantially across studies and were closely associated with study design, participant population, and technology maturity. Studies evaluating prototype systems under simulated conditions consistently reported higher classification performance than those conducted in real-world dementia care settings.

Among simulation-based studies, several machine learning models achieved near-perfect performance. Ziyad and colleagues [24] reported 100% accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score for fall detection using an AdaBoost ensemble classifier trained on wearable inertial sensor data. Similarly, Szántó and colleagues [23] achieved 100% accuracy when distinguishing between 35 simulated true falls and 70 false fall events using wearable sensors. Mishra and colleagues [21] likewise demonstrated high classification performance, reporting 95% accuracy with a decision tree classifier. Although these findings demonstrate the technical potential of machine learning-based fall detection, they were derived from healthy participants performing simulated falls under controlled laboratory conditions.

Studies involving clinically diagnosed people living with dementia reported more modest but clinically relevant performance. For fall prediction, Adeli and colleagues [26] demonstrated that ambient monitoring of gait characteristics predicted falls occurring within four weeks, achieving an area under the receiver operating characteristic (AUROC) of 0.762, sensitivity of 0.728, and specificity of 0.732. Similarly, Schwenk and colleagues (2015) [32] reported an area under curve (AUC) of 0.771 with 0.72 sensitivity and 0.76 specificity of predicting falls over a 3-month follow-up using wearable sensor-derived gait measures.

Several studies evaluated effectiveness using implementation- or patient-centered outcomes rather than algorithmic accuracy. Wright and colleagues [29] reported a 48% reduction in nighttime falls following implementation a vision-based monitoring system within a dementia care unit, while Taylor and colleagues [27] demonstrated acceptable usability of a tablet-based exercise intervention, with participant usability scores ranging from 68 to 69. These studies highlight that successful implementation may be reflected not only by predictive performance but also by meaningful improvements in safety, usability, and clinical outcomes.

sections.title: Technologies for fall detection, emergency response, and prevention

paragraphs.en: Wearable fall detection systems primarily rely on IMUs, accelerometers, and gyroscopes to identify biomechanical signatures, such as rapid orientation shifts followed by high-impact shocks, which are characteristic of falls. Under simulated conditions, these systems consistently demonstrated excellent classification performance. Mishra and colleagues [21] reported 95% accuracy using a finger-mounted IMU, while Ziyad and colleagues [24] and Szántó and colleagues [23] each achieved 100% accuracy when distinguishing simulated falls from activities of daily living using wearable sensor data.

Most wearable systems, however, were validated using healthy volunteers performing simulated falls rather than people living with dementia, limiting the generalizability of these findings to real-world clinical settings.

Ambient monitoring technologies eliminate the need for users to wear a device by continuously monitoring the environment using video, cameras, radar, or other environmental sensors. Yang and colleagues [20] demonstrated the utility of video-based monitoring in long-term care, reporting a modest 45.5% agreement between incident reports and video review regarding the cause of imbalance and 45.1% agreement for the activity being performed at the time of the fall. Similarly, Siedel and colleagues [19] evaluated an interactive ambient monitoring system that correctly detected 85% of 553 simulated falls.

Radar-based systems were also investigated as an alternative ambient sensing approach. In a three-month pilot study, Can and colleagues [31] reported that a commercial four-dimensional imaging radar system successfully detected all falls occurring within the intervention group, enabling immediate caregiver notification following fall events.

Several studies extended beyond detection to technologies designed to proactively reduce fall risk. Wright and colleagues [29] evaluated the Oxehealth vision-based monitoring platform in dementia care units and reported a 48% reduction in nighttime falls (p < 0.01), an 82% reduction in moderate-severity falls, a 68% reduction in emergency department admissions (p < 0.02), and a 49% reduction in paramedic visits. Wafiq and colleagues [22] developed a pressure-sensing system integrated into beds and chairs that achieved a 94.3% position identification rate and 96.4% precision for identifying high-risk positions associated with bed falls. Taylor and colleagues [27] evaluated a tablet-based exercise intervention and reported acceptable usability among participants, although the pilot data was not designed to assess reductions in fall incidence.

In summary, detection systems are advancing from wearable IMUs toward ambient, privacy-preserving radar, while prevention strategies increasingly integrate exergames and smart environments. The convergence of these approaches underscores the potential for comprehensive, proactive fall management tailored to the needs of people living with dementia.

This scoping review provides the first comprehensive synthesis of digital technologies developed for fall prediction, detection, and prevention specifically in people living with dementia. Across the thirteen included studies, we identified a rapidly evolving landscape of wearable sensors, ambient monitoring systems, computer vision platforms, radar technologies, and artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled algorithms designed to improve fall management. Collectively, these findings demonstrate considerable technological innovation and suggest that digital health technologies have the potential to support earlier risk identification, facilitate timely intervention following falls, and promote safer, more independent living for people living with dementia.

Despite these promising advances, our findings reveal a substantial gap between technological development and clinical translation. While many systems demonstrated excellent technical performance under controlled laboratory conditions, relatively few were evaluated in real-world dementia care settings, and even fewer examined sustained clinical effectiveness or implementation outcomes. Much of the current evidence remains derived from proof-of-concept studies, small pilot investigations, or simulated falls performed by healthy volunteers, limiting confidence in the generalizability of reported performance metrics to the complex clinical realities of dementia care.

Importantly, this review suggests that successful fall management extends beyond algorithmic accuracy. Although advances in AI and multimodal sensing have improved the ability to classify fall events and identify individuals at elevated risk, successful implementation ultimately depends on technologies that can be integrated into routine care while remaining acceptable to PlwD, caregivers, and healthcare providers. Accordingly, the next stage of innovation should prioritize clinical validation, user-centered design, implementation science, and long-term evaluation alongside continued technological development.

Overall, our findings indicate that the field is transitioning from demonstrating technical feasibility toward addressing the practical challenges of deployment in dementia care. Bridging this translational gap will require future research to move beyond optimizing predictive performance and instead evaluate how digital technologies influence clinically meaningful outcomes, including fall incidence, healthcare utilization, caregiver burden, quality of life, and the ability of people living with dementia to age safely in place.

sections.title: Methodological and implementation barriers to clinical translation
The “dementia gap”: Limited validation in representative clinical populations.

paragraphs.en: One of the most significant barriers to the clinical translation of fall management technologies is the persistent “dementia gap” in algorithm development and validation. Six of the thirteen included studies evaluated their technologies using healthy young adults performing simulated falls under controlled laboratory settings [19,21–25]. Although simulated datasets provide an efficient platform for early algorithm development, they fail to capture the complex motor, cognitive, and behavioral characteristics that distinguish falls in dementia.

Falls among people living with dementia arise within a fundamentally different biomechanical and neurological context. Progressive neurodegeneration impairs anticipatory postural adjustments, slows protective reflexes, and disrupts motor coordination, resulting in fall dynamics that differ substantially from the intentional, anticipated falls performed by healthy volunteers [7]. Altered gait initiation, increased stride-to-stride variability, and impaired balance further contribute to movement patterns that are unlikely to be adequately represented in simulated datasets [33]. Consequently, algorithms trained exclusively on healthy participants may identify movement patterns that do not accurately reflect falls occurring in routine dementia care.

This limitation is reflected in the reported performance of many prototype systems. Studies relying on simulated datasets frequently reported classification accuracies approaching 95%–100%, whereas studies conducted in clinical dementia population generally demonstrated more modest performance despite evaluating technologies under substantially more complex real-world conditions. This discrepancy suggests that current performance metrics may overestimate clinical applicability and reinforces the importance of validating technologies using representative dementia populations before widespread implementation.

Beyond population-specific validation, the field would benefit from more rigorous external validation of machine learning models. Most included studies evaluated algorithm performance using data collected from a single institution or experimental environment, with few assessing performances across independent populations, healthcare settings, or sensor platforms. Consequently, reported accuracy may not reflect performance following deployment in routine clinical practice. This challenge is compounded by the relatively small datasets used in many studies together with increasingly complex machine learning models, increasing the risk of overfitting whereby algorithms learn characteristics specific to the training dataset rather than generalizable fall-related movement patterns. Future research should therefore prioritize multicentre prospective validation, standardized benchmarking datasets, and external validation across diverse dementia populations to improve the robustness, reproducibility, and clinical generalizability of these technologies.

sections.title: The human factor: Usability, acceptability, and implementation.

paragraphs.en: Technical performance alone is insufficient to ensure successful implementation of fall management technologies. Rather, sustained adoption depends on whether technologies can be integrated into the daily lives of people living with dementia. Qualitative research and systematic reviews consistently reveal that devices are often designed without sufficient consideration for the lived experience of aging and dementia [34]. This review highlights that many implementation barriers arise not from algorithmic limitations but from challenges related to usability, acceptability, and long-term adherence.

Wearable technologies exemplify this disconnect between technical capability and real-world implementation. Although inertial sensor systems demonstrated promising predictive performance [21,28], their effectiveness depends on consistent use. Cognitive impairment, memory deficits, behavioral symptoms, sensory sensitivities, and reduced dexterity may all compromise adherence by making devices uncomfortable, difficult to manage or easy to forget [35]. Consequently, technologies that perform well under experimental conditions may experience substantially reduced effectiveness when deployed in routine dementia care.

Although many studies reported high accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity, these metrics alone may not adequately reflect clinical usefulness. False-positive alerts may contribute to alarm fatigue among caregivers and healthcare staff, potentially reducing trust in monitoring systems and diminishing long-term adherence. Conversely, false-negative events may delay emergency response following a fall. Future evaluations should therefore incorporate implementation outcomes such as false alarm rates, caregiver workload, response time, usability, and user satisfaction in addition to conventional algorithmic performance metrics.

Collectively, these findings suggest that the primary barriers to clinical translation are no longer solely technological. Rather, they reflect the need to develop systems that are externally validated, clinically implementable, and acceptable to the people who will ultimately use them. Advancing the field will therefore require greater integration of engineering, clinical science, implementation science, and user-centered design to ensure that technological innovation translates into meaningful improvements in dementia care.

Although many technologies demonstrated promising technical performance, relatively few have generated the level of evidence required for widespread clinical implementation. For a digital health intervention to become standard of care, it must demonstrate technical feasibility and meaningful improvements in patient outcomes, scalability, and economic value under real-world conditions. Our review indicates that the current evidence base falls substantially short of these requirements.

The literature remains dominated by feasibility studies, proof-of-concept investigations, and small observational cohorts, with a notable absence of adequately powered randomized controlled trials evaluating clinically meaningful outcomes. While many studies reported excellent algorithmic performance, few assessed whether these technologies ultimately reduced fall incidence, injury severity, hospitalization, institutionalization, or mortality. Wright and colleagues [29] represents a notable exception, demonstrating a 48% reduction in nighttime falls using a vision-based monitoring system within a dementia care setting. However, studies of this scale and clinical relevance remain uncommon, limiting confidence in the effectiveness of most technologies beyond controlled research environments.

An equally important evidence gap related to economic evaluation. Although some studies have modeled the potential cost-effectiveness of general fall prevention programs like exercise [36], and others have shown digital exercise apps to be cost-saving [37], there is little to no data on the specific return on investment of most new detection or monitoring technologies in dementia care [38]. This limitation represents a critical barrier to implementation, as healthcare organizations increasingly require evidence that digital innovations improve outcomes while remaining financially sustainable. Future research should therefore incorporate formal health economic analyses alongside clinical effectiveness evaluations, considering implementation costs, maintenance requirements, caregiver workload, and downstream savings associated with reduced hospitalizations, delayed institutionalization, and avoided emergency department visits.

More broadly, our findings suggest that fall management technologies are evolving beyond stand-alone detection systems toward integrated digital models of care. Rather than functioning solely as passive fall detectors, future technologies may become components of comprehensive digital care pathways that integrate continuous monitoring, risk prediction, remote rehabilitation, and longitudinal clinical follow-up. Such models have the potential to facilitate earlier intervention, improve continuity of care, and support more proactive, person-centered management of fall risk in people living with dementia.

Collectively, these findings indicate that the principal challenge facing the field is no longer technological innovation but successful implementation. Bridging this gap will require rigorous effectiveness trials, standardized economic evaluations, and implementation science approaches that demonstrate not only whether these technologies work, but how they can be sustainably integrated into routine dementia care.

The deployment of continuous monitoring technologies within the homes and care environments of people living with dementia raises ethical challenges that extend beyond technical performance. Unlike many other digital health applications, fall management systems frequently operate within highly private spaces and collect continuous behavioral or physiological data from individuals with progressive cognitive impairment. Consequently, successful implementation requires not only technological effectiveness, but also careful consideration of privacy, autonomy, dignity, and public trust.

The central ethical challenge is balancing patient safety with the preservation of privacy and personal autonomy [39]. Technologies capable of providing the richest contextual information, including video- and audio-based monitoring systems, may facilitate more accurate fall detection but are also among the most intrusive, with many users and caregivers expressing concerns regarding surveillance, dignity, and loss of privacy [15]. These concerns have accelerated the development of privacy-preserving alternatives, including four-dimensional imaging radar, depth cameras, thermal imaging, and passive infrared sensors, which enable continuous movement monitoring while minimizing the collection of personally identifiable information. As demonstrated by several studies included in this review, privacy-preserving sensing technologies may offer an important compromise between maintaining patient safety and respecting individual dignity.

Beyond privacy, dementia introduces unique challenges surrounding informed consent and decision-making capacity. Traditional models of one-time informed consent are unlikely to remain sufficient throughout the course of a progressive neurodegenerative disease, as an individual’s capacity to understand ongoing monitoring and exercise autonomous decision-making may change over time [40]. Ethical frameworks must therefore evolve from a static concept of consent to a dynamic process of continual assent, involving ongoing conversations and shared decision-making with the person with dementia, their family, and their legal proxies [39]. Such approaches better reflect the dynamic nature of cognitive decline while preserving autonomy whenever possible.

These considerations are increasingly reflected within international digital health governance frameworks. The World Health Organization’s Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health emphasizes transparency, accountability, human oversight, and proportionality as fundamental principles for responsible AI implementation in healthcare [41]. Similarly, the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation highlights data minimization, privacy by design, and explicit governance of sensitive health data, while longstanding frameworks such as the Belmont Report continues to provide foundational ethical principles of autonomy, beneficence, and justice as ethical imperatives [42]. Aligning future fall management technologies with these established frameworks may facilitate regulatory approval, increase clinician and caregiver confidence, and promote responsible translation into routine dementia care.

Ultimately, ethical considerations should be viewed as essential design requirements. Technologies that are transparent, privacy-preserving, and developed with sustained engagement from people living with dementia, caregivers, clinicians, and policymakers are likely to achieve greater trust, acceptability, and long-term adoption. Integrating ethical principles throughout the technology development lifecycle will therefore be critical to ensuring that digital innovation enhances safety while preserving dignity and person-centered care.

The findings of this review should be interpreted within the context of both its strengths and its inherent methodological limitations. As an emerging field, digital fall management for people living with dementia is characterized by rapidly evolving technologies, heterogeneous study designs, and limited high-quality clinical evidence. Consequently, while this review provides a comprehensive synthesis of the current landscape, several considerations are important when interpreting its findings.

Our review has several notable strengths. To our knowledge, this is the first scoping review to comprehensively synthesize primary evidence on technologies for fall prediction, detection, and prevention specifically for people living with dementia. By integrating evidence across engineering, digital health, geriatrics, and dementia care, we provide a broad overview of the current technological landscape while identifying methodological, clinical, ethical, and implementation challenges that may influence future translation into practice. Furthermore, the review was conducted using established Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and reported in accordance with the PRISMA-ScR guidelines, enhancing methodological transparency and reproducibility.

As for limitations, first, the findings should be interpreted in the context of the limited and heterogeneous evidence base currently available. Only 13 studies met the eligibility criteria, encompassing diverse study designs, populations, technologies, outcome measures, and validation approaches. This heterogeneity precluded quantitative synthesis and limited direct comparisons between technologies. Consequently, our findings should be interpreted as mapping the current state of the evidence rather than establishing comparative effectiveness, as would be appropriate for a subsequent systematic review and meta-analysis once the field is more established with a robust number of randomized controlled trials.

Second, many of the included studies were early-stage feasibility or proof-of-concept investigations involving relatively small sample sizes, short follow-up periods, or simulated falls performed by healthy participants rather than people living with dementia. As discussed previously, these methodological limitations reduce the generalizability of reported performance metrics and may overestimate the clinical performance of emerging technologies when implemented in routine dementia care.

Despite current challenges, the future of fall management technology will be shaped by the development of more intelligent, personalized, and clinically meaningful systems. First, future research must address the limited maturity and heterogeneity of the current evidence base. Although this review identified all eligible studies, only thirteen investigations met inclusion criteria, reflecting the early stage of the field. Existing studies vary substantially in design, populations, sensing modalities, algorithms, and outcome measures, with many remaining proof-of-concept studies conducted in controlled environments using simulated falls or small convenience samples. Larger, longitudinal, real-world evaluations are therefore needed to establish generalizability, clinical utility, and comparative effectiveness.

Second, the field should continue shifting from reactive fall detection toward proactive fall prediction and prevention through artificial intelligence and predictive analytics. By integrating longitudinal, multimodal data, including gait, activity patterns, sleep, and physiological measures, AI systems may establish individualized baselines and identify early deviations associated with increased fall risk, enabling timely interventions before falls occur [43]. However, as AI adoption expands, predictive performance must be accompanied by transparency and interpretability. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) approaches will be critical for improving clinician trust, supporting regulatory acceptance, and ensuring that predictions meaningfully inform rather than replace clinical decision-making. Beyond fall detection and monitoring, emerging technology-assisted assessment and telemedicine-enabled rehabilitation models in neurological populations may offer opportunities to integrate remote assessment, longitudinal monitoring, and personalized intervention into future dementia care pathways [44–46]. However, dementia-specific validation remains necessary before these approaches can be translated into routine practice.

Third, future technologies should prioritize multimodal sensor integration and comprehensive care platforms. Current evidence remains dominated by single-modality systems, particularly wearable inertial measurement units, despite the potential advantages of combining complementary technologies such as wearables, radar, and vision-based sensors. Advancing sensor fusion approaches, as demonstrated by studies such as Adeli et al. [26], may improve robustness and accuracy in complex real-world environments. Concurrently, the field should move beyond fragmented, single-purpose ‘point solutions’ toward integrated platforms. Instead of requiring a person with dementia and their caregiver to manage a disparate collection of devices for falls, medication, and communication, these functions should be consolidated into unified systems, such as comprehensive smart home networks or multi-functional smartwatches [47]. This approach simplifies the user experience, reduces the overall technology burden, and allows for the creation of more holistic care and support ecosystems.

Fourth, future evaluations must extend beyond technical performance metrics to examine meaningful clinical and patient-centered outcomes. Research should determine whether these technologies improve independence, mobility, quality of life, caregiver burden, and long-term care outcomes among people living with dementia.

Finally, successful implementation will require a shift toward user-centered co-design approaches, involving people living with dementia, caregivers, and healthcare professionals throughout the technology development lifecycle [48]. Collaborative development processes encompassing needs assessment, prototyping, usability testing, and implementation planning are essential to ensure that future innovations are not only technically effective but also acceptable, accessible, and sustainable within dementia care.

Technology holds immense potential to transform fall management in people living with dementia by enabling objective, continuous, and personalized approaches to risk assessment, detection, and prevention. Emerging innovations, including wearable biosensors, privacy-preserving ambient systems, and interactive virtual reality interventions, demonstrate promising applications. However, real-world evidence remains limited. Current literature is dominated by small-scale feasibility studies, often constrained by methodological heterogeneity, and a persistent dementia validation gap, leaving uncertainty regarding usability, acceptability, clinical benefit, scalability and long-term impact.

Future progress requires a shift beyond proof-of-concept research toward rigorous, longitudinal evaluations in representative dementia populations using standardized outcomes and transparent reporting. Successful translation will depend on human-centered co-design, integration of multimodal and privacy-preserving technologies, and evaluation of meaningful outcomes including falls, injuries, healthcare utilization, caregiver burden, and quality of life. Clinicians, researchers, technologists, and policymakers must work collaboratively to ensure that validated technologies are implemented as part of comprehensive, person-centered dementia care. By aligning technological innovation with clinical evidence, cost-effectiveness, and usability, gerontechnology can meaningfully enhance safety, independence, and dignity for the growing population of people living with dementia.

tables.caption: Technology and methodological characteristics of dementia-targeted fall management technologies.
rows: Combining a microcontroller (STM32 L412KB), communication module (LoRa S76G with GPS), accelerometer/gyroscope (GY-521), PPG heart rate sensor, and a fingerprint reader into a single device.

The fall detection system achieved 100% accuracy in distinguishing between simulated true falls and false falls (activities like sitting, lying down, and jumping) across 7 participants performing a total of 105 actions (35 true falls, 70 false falls).
Custom-built device using an Arduino Nicla SENSE ME board.
The optimal model, a Decision Tree classifier, achieved an accuracy (r-squared score) of 95% in detecting simulated falls.
ML algorithms: logistic regression, random forest, decision tree, Gaussian Naïve Baye’s, SVM, and K neighbours classifier.
Accelerometer, gyroscope, magnetometer, IMU (ankle, thigh, head, sternum, and waist)

The AdaBoost ensemble classifier and the K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) classifier both achieved 100% accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score for classifying falls versus activities of daily living on the IMU dataset.

A prediction model combining a history of previous falls with a sensor-derived measure of 'walking bout average duration' (<15 s) achieved an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.771 (p ≤ 0.001). This model predicted falls over a 3-month period with 72% sensitivity and 76% specificity, and an odds ratio of 7.71.
Real-time, caregiver alert, clinician dashboard, and alarm

During the 3-month follow-up, there were 2 falls in the control group and 1 fall in the study group. The fall in the study group was detected by the device, which notified staff for a prompt response. The falls in the control group were identified retrospectively by staff with no immediate attention.
Radar-based fall detection algorithm with signal-processing and pattern-recognition methods (proprietary to Vayyar).
Microsoft Kinect for Windows v2 as a depth sensor was combined with an RFID system to identify which study participant’s gait was being recorded.

The best performing ML model predicted falls over the subsequent 4 weeks with an AUROC of 0.762, sensitivity of 0.728, and specificity of 0.732.The model that excluded the ambient gait features only achieved an F1-score of 56.2%, highlighting the significant contribution of the ambient monitoring data. The model achieved its highest AUROC of 77.4% when predicting falls over a 5-week period.
A two-layered MLP as the binary classifier, through SVM, logistic regression, and random forest models were also tested. SMOTE was employed to address imbalanced data.

Significant 48% reduction in nighttime falls (P < 0.01). Visits from paramedics were reduced by 49% (P < 0.2). Accident & Emergency (A&E) admissions were reduced by 68% (P < 0.02). Moderate severity falls were reduced by 82%. Enhanced one-to-one observation hours were reduced by 71%.
Custom-built Ambient Assisted Living (AAL) system named AUXILIA
RGB camera (omnidirectional camera), infrared, microphone (wall/ceiling mounted), speech recognition component (vicControl DSP 3.2)
The interactive fall detection system achieved a correct detection rate of 85% on a dataset of 553 simulated falls.

Small-scale dementia care home was a highly successful and satisfactory model for guests, families, and staff because its use of technology supported an overall philosophy of care that empowered staff, promoted a sense of community, and maximized the choice and dignity of risk for residents.

There was a significant discrepancy between incident reports and video analysis. Agreement was 45.5% for the cause of imbalance, 45.1% for the activity at the time of the fall, and 79.5% for the use of mobility aids.
Force sensitive resistors combined with an Arduino Mega 2560 microcontroller, an ESP-32 module, and the Blynk IoT platform for remote monitoring and alerts

The final optimized system achieved an overall position identification rate of 94.29%. For the specific task of identifying risky positions, it achieved a precision of 0.964, a recall of 0.900, and an F1-Score of 0.931.
Combining Interlink Electronics for the pressure sensors, Arduino for the signal processing module, and RN171 for the Wi-Fi module.
Real-time, caregiver alert, clinician dashboard, and alarm

No numeric results are provided. The study demonstrated through experimental testing that the prototype could successfully distinguish between simulated normal walking (4–6 sensors activated, no alarm) and simulated falls (>7 sensors activated, alarm triggered). It also successfully visualized simulated wandering patterns on the user interface.
Threshold-based: If 7 or more sensors are activated, Arduino then triggers alerts (LED + buzzer) and transmits the information via Wi-Fi to a LabVIEW-based human-machine interface.
Exercise program to improve gait control

The program demonstrated acceptable feasibility with mean System Usability Scale scores of 68 ± 21 for participants and 69 ± 15 for caregivers, a mean Physical Activity Enjoyment Scale score of 44 ± 8, and an average of 65 exercise minutes in week 12.

The app provides an individually tailored and progressive exercise program, adjusting training intensity based on user-reported Rate of Perceived Exertion ratings after each exercise to ensure the training remains challenging but safe.
